questions.question: For a finite connected undirected network, which condition on the vertex degrees is equivalent to the existence of an Euler tour?
options: At most two vertices have odd degree.
Every vertex has degree exactly 2.
The total number of edges is even.
Every single vertex has even degree.

questions.question: A finite connected undirected network has an Euler tour. Which argument shows that every vertex of the network must have even degree?
options: The tour visits every vertex exactly once, so it uses exactly two of the edges at each vertex.
Each pass pairs an arriving edge with a departing edge, and the start pairs its first exit with the final return.
The degrees of all vertices sum to twice the number of edges, so each single degree is even.
An undirected edge is used once in each direction, so it adds two edge ends at every vertex it meets.

questions.question: A student claims: every finite connected undirected network in which each vertex has degree at least 2 has an Euler tour. Which network is a counterexample to this claim?
options: The triangle A–B–C with edges A–B, B–C, C–A
The cycle A–B–C–D–A with the extra edge A–C
Two triangles A–B–C and A–D–E sharing only A
The path A–B–C–D with edges A–B, B–C, C–D

questions.question: In a finite connected undirected network every vertex has even degree. One edge joining two different vertices $u$ and $v$ is deleted, and the network stays connected. What can be said about an Euler tour of the new network?
options: None exists, since every vertex now has odd degree.
One exists, since the network is still connected.
None exists, since $u$ and $v$ now have odd degree.
One exists, since $u$ and $v$ each lose two edge ends.

questions.question: An undirected network has vertices A, B, C, D, E and edges A–B, A–C, B–C, B–D, C–D, C–E, D–E. Does it have an Euler tour, and why?
options: No, because B and D have odd degree 3.
Yes, because only two vertices have odd degree.
Yes, because the network is connected.
No, because C has degree 4 and is passed twice.

questions.question: An undirected network has vertices P, Q, R, two parallel edges between P and Q, one edge Q–R and one edge R–P. Does the network have an Euler tour?
options: Yes: P, Q and R each have degree 2.
No: P and Q both have odd degree 3.
No: parallel edges are never allowed in a tour.
Yes: exactly two vertices have odd degree.

questions.question: In a connected undirected network with an Euler tour, a vertex $v$ that is not the start of the tour has degree 6. How many times does the tour pass through $v$?
options: Exactly 6 times, once for each incident edge
Exactly once, since a tour visits each vertex once
Between 1 and 3 times, depending on the route
Exactly 3 times, using two incident edges per pass

questions.question: An undirected network consists of the cycle A–B–C–D–A and the cycle A–E–F–A, which share only vertex A. Does the network have an Euler tour?
options: No: the tour would have to pass vertex A twice.
No: two separate cycles cannot form one closed route.
No: the network has 7 edges, an odd number.
Yes: A has degree 4 and all other vertices degree 2.

questions.question: A finite connected undirected network with at least one edge has every vertex of even degree. A route must start and end at a prescribed vertex $v$ and use every edge exactly once. When does such a route exist?
options: Always: the tour passes $v$, so it can start there.
Only if $v$ has odd degree, as the tour starts there.
Not always: a tour begun elsewhere cannot be restarted at $v$.
Only if $v$ has degree 2, so it opens and closes it.

questions.question: In a connected undirected network the only odd-degree vertices are $U$ and $W$. A parallel copy is added to each edge of the path $U$–$X$–$Y$–$W$. Why do $X$ and $Y$ still have even degree?
options: Parallel copies are not counted in the degree, so $X$ and $Y$ are unchanged.
Each of $X$ and $Y$ lies on two copied edges, so each gains two edge ends.
$X$ and $Y$ gain one edge end each, which turns their odd degree even.
Copying the path adds edge ends only at its endpoints $U$ and $W$.

questions.question: A gritting lorry must drive along every two-way street of a town exactly once and return to its depot. Junctions are vertices and street segments between junctions are edges of an undirected network. Which check decides whether such a route exists?
options: The network is connected and the total number of street segments is even.
Every junction meets at least two street segments, so the lorry can always leave it.
Every junction except the depot meets an even number of street segments.
The network is connected and every junction meets an even number of street segments.

questions.question: A connected undirected network on vertices P, Q, R, S, T has degrees $\deg P=4$, $\deg Q=3$, $\deg R=4$, $\deg S=3$, $\deg T=4$, and Q and S are not adjacent. Which addition of new edges makes it an Euler network?
options: One new edge joining Q and S
One new edge joining P and Q
One parallel copy of the edge R–T
Two parallel new edges joining Q and S

questions.question: Four land areas are joined by seven bridges, giving a connected undirected network with degrees 5, 3, 3 and 3. New bridges may be built between existing land areas. What is the smallest number of new bridges after which a closed walk crossing every bridge exactly once exists?
options: 1 new bridge
4 new bridges
2 new bridges
3 new bridges

questions.question: A connected undirected network has 6 vertices and 9 edges. Five of the vertices have degrees 2, 4, 2, 4 and 2; the degree of the sixth was not recorded. Does the network have an Euler tour?
options: Yes: the sixth degree is $18-14=4$, so all are even.
It cannot be decided without knowing the sixth degree.
No: with 9 edges, some vertex has odd degree.
No: the average degree $18/6=3$ is odd.

questions.question: Consider finite undirected networks that need not be connected. For such a network, how does the condition 'every vertex has even degree' relate to the existence of an Euler tour?
options: Even degrees are needed for a tour but do not guarantee one.
Even degrees guarantee a tour, yet a tour can exist without them.
Even degrees hold exactly when an Euler tour exists.
A tour can occur with odd degrees, and even ones guarantee nothing.

questions.question: Take any finite connected undirected network and add a parallel copy of every edge. When does the resulting network have an Euler tour?
options: Only when the original network already had all degrees even.
Always, since every degree is doubled and is therefore even.
Only when the original network had exactly two odd vertices.
Never, since parallel copies are counted only once in a degree.

questions.question: The complete network on $n\ge 3$ vertices has exactly one undirected edge between every pair of vertices. For which $n$ does it have an Euler tour?
options: Exactly when $n$ is even, the number of vertices.
For every $n\ge3$, since the network is connected.
Exactly when $n$ is odd, since each degree is $n-1$.
Exactly when the edge count $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ is even.

questions.question: A network consists of triangle A–B–C, triangle D–E–F and one extra edge C–D. Exactly one edge is to be deleted so that the remaining network has an Euler tour. Which deletion achieves this?
options: Delete C–D: afterwards every vertex has even degree, so a tour exists.
Delete A–C: this makes C even, which removes the obstruction at C.
None: only C–D could work, and deleting it disconnects the network.
No deletion is needed: two odd vertices still allow a closed tour.
